title: Noting spreads
hookLine: Mahasi Sayadaw's method of noting travels far beyond Burma

cards: Falling. Two words, said silently, over and over, in a meditation hall in Burma or on another continent. A person sits, sometimes with a hand on the belly.
As the belly lifts with the in-breath: rising. As it sinks: falling. A sound from outside.
Hearing, hearing. An itch on the cheek. Itching.

teach.b: First, the home base. Mahasi built his teaching on the old instructions of the Satipatthana Sutta, to be mindful of body, feelings, mind and the things the mind meets.
He made the start simple: one place to return to, the rise and fall of the belly, again and again.

teach.h: A SOFT LABEL, NOT A JUDGMENT.
teach.b: Second, the label. Whatever pulls attention away gets a plain word, not a judgment or a story, just a name for what's happening: hearing, itching, wanting, worrying.
The note is made silently, and teachers in his line describe it as light, a whisper rather than a shout.
Naming a sound as hearing keeps you from building a whole argument about the neighbor's car; the label catches the moment before the story starts. Third, walking.
In Mahasi centers, practice doesn't stop when you stand up.

Students walk slowly back and forth, noting each step: lifting, moving, placing. They alternate sitting and walking through the day, so attention carries from the cushion to the floor to the dining hall.
Fourth, how it traveled. Mahasi's students, monks and lay people both, carried the method to centers in other countries, and teachers there adapted it.
Some keep careful labels for everything; some use them only when the mind gets lost.
Plain enough to travel and flexible enough to change: that's how rising, falling came to be whispered in halls a long way from where Mahasi taught.

how: In Mahasi-style retreats, meditators alternate periods of sitting, noting the rise and fall of the abdomen, with slow walking, noting each part of each step, often for whole days in silence.

games.q: you're sitting, noting rising, falling. a car alarm starts outside. what does Mahasi's method ask of you?
o: block it out and keep saying rising.
note hearing, hearing, then return to the belly.
stop sitting until it's quiet again.
games.why: the sound isn't fought or followed. it's noted, hearing, hearing, and then attention goes back to rising, falling.

practice: Find the movement of your belly as you breathe, resting a hand there if it helps, and silently note rising as it lifts and falling as it sinks.
When something pulls you away, give it one soft word, hearing, thinking, itching, planning, then come back to rising, falling. No need to note perfectly, or to note everything; a whisper is enough.

wordCard.voice: Noting spreads. Mahasi Sayadaw's method: rising, falling, and a soft label for whatever pulls you away, carried by his students far beyond Burma. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sati: mindfulness, remembering to be present. noting is one way to keep it going.

carryVoice: Your line: rising, falling. One plain word can catch the moment. That's today, done.
